newsitem.title: USA: US Energy Dept declines comment on staff shuffle.
newsitem.headline: US Energy Dept declines comment on staff shuffle.

text.p: The U.S. Department of Energy refused to comment Friday on a report that Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary was moving to get rid of some political appointees before Federico Pena took over the energy reins.
The Houston Chronicle reported that O'Leary had urged Assistant Secretary Christine Ervin, nuclear nonproliferation director Joan Rohlfing, and research director Martha Krebs to leave.
"We have no official word on the status of DOE officials other than the secretary herself," said a spokeswoman.
But Energy Department officials said O'Leary would not take action without the White House's backing.
"Personnel decisions for political appointments are made at the White House," said the Energy Department spokeswoman.
An administration official said rumors of the moves had "raised consternation at the White House."

"In general there is a dispute about whether the Secretary of Energy should be making personnel changes in the midst of a transition," he said. "It's frankly unclear how that dispute will be resolved."
Ervin had no comment on her status. Her assistant, Jesse Ulin, said: "I am unaware of whether or not Ervin is leaving."
Krebs said she had not talked to O'Leary, her staff, or the White House about leaving, and added that while her job had been "uncomfortable" at times, she was happy.

Rohlfing declined to comment. Another administration official said O'Leary had "had conversations" with Rohlfing, Ervin and others, but nothing had been issued in writing. Environmentalists were nervous about what an exit by Ervin, a major advocate for energy efficiency and renewable fuels, might mean for the Clinton administration's agenda.
"It certainly doesn't bode well for where the administration is going on environmental issues," said Dan Becker, energy program director for the Sierra Club.
Some suggested that Ervin's clash with the natural gas industry over a home energy rating system dimmed her prospects at the department.

The rating system had sparked fury in the natural gas industry which claimed that the system would have wrongly favored electricity as more efficient than natural gas, despite higher costs and inefficiencies in producing electricity. The issue became moot when Congress cut all funding for the rating system.
